newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh faces criticism over slow reforms.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh faces criticism over slow reforms.

text.p: A World Bank official said the sluggish pace of Bangladesh's economic reforms was likely to lead to a reduction in aid and strong criticism from donor countries at a conference later this year.

The Bangladesh Aid Consortium meeting in Dhaka next November will focus on the progress of reforms in macroeconomics, private sector development, poverty alleviation and selling or winding up loss-making state-owned companies, the World Bank official told Reuters on Friday.

"The level of pledging (of aid) will come down in comparison to previous years," said the official, who requested anonymity. "Such pledging is ... a political game for the government. We cannot do it anymore.
"The reforms have been slow ... and the government will have to face criticism over its failure," he said.

Bangladesh will seek fresh foreign aid commitment for fiscal 1997/98 (July-June) at the two-day consortium meeting on November 3 in Dhaka under World Bank sponsorship. The meeting will include representatives of the United States, Japan and other donor countries.
"We will request $2.3 billion from the donors for 1997/98," said an official with the government's Economic Relations Division.
"The government is determined to implement the reforms in phases," he told Reuters on Thursday.

The World Bank official said that at the Dhaka meeting "the private sector for the first time would be invited to participate in the dialogue actively and the donors would listen to them about their problems".
He said before any fresh commitments were made the donors would make by-case appraisals of each aid project with the relevant Bangladeshi ministries.
He said the process of commitment would be more complicated because management of aid by Bangladesh in the past was "not satisfactory".

The last consortium meeting, held in Paris in September 1996, pledged $2.1 billion for Bangladesh in 1996/97. The World Bank at the time expressed hope that Dhaka would complete reforms "faster and in time".
Finance Ministry officials said Dhaka sought the disbursement of at least $1.7 billion in the current fiscal year, but that disbursements so far were well below that. They would not give details.
Donors pledged $1.95 billion for 1995/96 but actual disbursement was $1.59 billion, they said.
At a mid-term review of Bangladesh's aid utilisation and reforms in Dhaka in February, the country faced strong criticism for the slow pace of economic reform.
